title: The half-life of mean reversion
objectives: Estimate how fast a series mean-reverts from its AR(1) coefficient
Put an interval on a half-life and test for a unit root first

screens.title: Halfway home
screens.prose: Two spreads start 3 units above their mean of 0: $x_0 = 3$, then $x_t = \phi x_{t-1} + 0.3\,\varepsilon_t$, with the same seeded shocks (seed 7) for both. One has $\phi = 0.9$, the other $\phi = 0.98$. The dashed lines are the average paths, $3\phi^t$.
screens.question: On average, which spread is halfway back first, and after about how long?

options.why: You took 10% of the *starting* gap off each day: 0.3 a day for 5 days. Each day removes 10% of what is *left*, so the steps shrink.
A $\phi$ near 1 keeps 98% of the gap each day: more memory, slower return.

hints.text: Which dashed line crosses the halfway line first?
Follow the blue dashed line down to 1.5.
It crosses between days 6 and 7; the green one takes about 34 days.

feedback.correct: Correct. About 6.6 days for $\phi = 0.9$, about 34 for $\phi = 0.98$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read where each dashed line meets 1.5.

explain.text: $3 \times 0.9^t$ falls to 1.5 at $t \approx 6.6$; $3 \times 0.98^t$ needs about 34 days. The noisy paths cross by luck on days 5 and 16 here; the average path sets the clock. A small change in $\phi$ near 1 changes the wait a lot.

screens.title: The decay curve
screens.prose: The curve is $\phi^h$: the share of a deviation still left after $h$ days. Move $\phi$, then drag the point along the curve to where it crosses one half.
screens.question: At $\phi = 0.95$, about how many days until half the deviation is gone?

options.why: You took 5% of the starting gap off each day, so 10 days for half. Each day takes 5% of what is left, which takes longer.
At 20 days $0.95^{20} = 0.36$ is left: past halfway already.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set $\phi = 0.95$ and drag the point to the line at one half.

explain.text: At $\phi = 0.95$ the curve crosses one half at $h \approx 13.5$ days. At 0.9 it is 6.6, at 0.98 about 34. The crossing is the **half-life** of a deviation.

screens.title: The half-life
screens.prose: The **half-life** is the $h$ with $\phi^h = \tfrac12$. Taking logs gives $$h = \frac{\ln 0.5}{\ln \phi}.$$ Both logs are negative for $0 < \phi < 1$, so $h$ is positive.
screens.question: What is the half-life for $\phi = 0.8$, in days? Give 3 places.

hints.text: Divide one log by the other.

byKey.linear: You took 20% of the starting gap off each day. The decay is geometric: 20% of what is left.
byKey.flip: You divided the other way round. $h = \ln 0.5 / \ln \phi$.
byKey.life: That is $1/(1 - \phi)$, a rough average lifetime, not the time to half.

screens.title: Steep near one
screens.prose: Half-lives on a log scale, in days, labelled by $\phi$. Moving $\phi$ from 0.95 to 0.99 multiplies the half-life by five.
screens.question: Drag the point to the half-life for $\phi = 0.98$.

byKey.linear: You used $0.5/(1 - \phi) = 25$ days, a straight-line decay. Geometric decay is slower: 34.31 days.

explain.text: $\ln 0.5/\ln 0.98 = 34.31$ days. Near 1, $\ln\phi \approx \phi - 1$, so the half-life is about $0.693/(1 - \phi)$: halving the distance to 1 doubles the wait.

screens.title: Any fraction
screens.prose: Generalise: the days until a deviation shrinks to `frac` of itself solve $|\phi|^h = \text{frac}$. Return `math.inf` when $|\phi| \ge 1$, since the deviation never shrinks, and 0.0 when $\phi = 0$. A negative $\phi$ flips sides each day, so its size decays at rate $|\phi|$.

screens.title: Estimating $\phi$
screens.prose: On data we estimate $\phi$ by the Dickey-Fuller regression from level 1: $$\Delta x_t = a + b\,x_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t, \qquad b = \phi - 1.$$ Here $x_t$ is a seeded pairs spread over 1,000 days, with a true $\phi = 0.95$. It is the residual of $y$ on $x$ from `make_pair(3, 1000)`.
screens.question: What half-life does this estimate give, in days? Give 2 places.

feedback.correct: Correct. About 13.3 days, against a true 13.51.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $\hat\phi = 1 + b$ in $\ln 0.5/\ln\hat\phi$.

byKey.slope: You put the slope $b$ itself into the log. The regression slope is $\phi - 1$; use $\ln(1 + b)$.
byKey.approx: That is the approximation $\ln 2/|b|$. Close, but the exact form uses $\ln(1 + b)$: 13.29.
byKey.true: That is the true half-life of the simulation. The data give an estimate.

explain.text: $\hat\phi = 1 + b = 0.9492$, so the half-life is $\ln 0.5/\ln 0.9492 = 13.288$ days. The true value is 13.513. `coint` lesson 7 runs this same estimate on a cointegrating spread.

widget.solution:
import math
import numpy as np

def half_life_ci(x, z=1.96):
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    dx = np.diff(x)
    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(dx)), x[:-1]])
    beta = np.linalg.lstsq(X, dx, rcond=None)[0]
    resid = dx - X @ beta
    s2 = resid @ resid / (len(dx) - 2)
    se = math.sqrt(s2 * np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X)[1, 1])        # standard error of b
    def hl(b):
        return math.inf if b >= 0 else math.log(0.5) / math.log(1 + b)
    b = beta[1]
    return (round(hl(b - z * se), 2), round(hl(b + z * se), 2))   # low b gives the short end

tests.setup: px, py = make_pair(3, 1000); X = np.column_stack([np.ones(1000), px]); u = py - X @ np.linalg.lstsq(X, py, rcond=None)[0]

screens.title: Worth trading?
screens.prose: A pairs desk has three spreads, each passing the ADF test. Estimated half-lives: A, 4 days; B, 13 days (the spread above, interval 10 to 22); C, 110 days. The desk can fund a position for at most 20 trading days, and a quarter is about 63.
screens.question: Which spreads suit the desk?

options.text: A and B; C reverts too slowly to fund
All three: each passes the ADF test
options.why: You stopped at the test. Stationarity is necessary but not enough. C takes 110 days to close half its gap, far past the 20 the desk can fund.

options.text: A only: B's interval reaches 22 days, past the limit
options.why: You treated the upper end as the estimate. B's central half-life is 13 days, and even at 22 days half the gap closes within about a month.

hints.text: Compare each half-life with the funding period.
A half-life longer than the holding period means most of the gap is still open when the money runs out.

feedback.correct: Correct. Speed matters as much as stationarity.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set each half-life beside the 20-day funding limit.

explain.text: Pairs desks skip a spread whose half-life exceeds the holding period they can fund, or a quarter. `coint` lesson 7 estimates this same number on a cointegrating spread. A half-life that grows on rolling windows warns that the pair is breaking, as `coint` lesson 11 shows.

ideas: A deviation decays like $\phi^h$, so it halves in $h = \ln 0.5/\ln\phi$ days.
Estimate $\phi$ with the regression $\Delta x_t = a + b\,x_{t-1}$, $\hat\phi = 1 + b$, and map the interval of $b$ to an interval of half-lives.
Near $\phi = 1$ the map is steep: small errors in $\hat\phi$ mean large errors in days.

formula.name: Half-life
formula.note: None for $\phi \ge 1$; use $|\phi|$ for a negative $\phi$.

summary.trap: A half-life of a series that fails the ADF test is a number about reversion that never happens.

quiz.question: What is the half-life of the size of its deviation, in days?

byKey.nan: You gave up because $\ln(-0.6)$ is undefined. The size of the gap decays by $|\phi|$.
byKey.one: One day is the flip, not the halving.
